title: Sunday schools
hook: Robert Raikes starts schools on Sundays for children working in factories the rest of the week

segments.voice: Yesterday, Wilberforce, pressing the case against the slave trade again and again. Your line was you cannot say you did not know.
screen: `YOU CANNOT SAY YOU DID NOT KNOW.`

segments.voice: One day a week, the machines in an English factory town go quiet, and the children who work them are out in the streets: loud, ragged, bored, getting into fights, with no school to go to and no one to stop them. Neighbors complain. A newspaper man in Gloucester, Robert Raikes, looks at the same children and asks a different question. Not how do we keep them quiet, but what if they could read?

Today Sunday school can mean a cheerful hour of Bible stories while the grown-ups are in church. It began as something tougher. Raikes's children worked during the week. Sunday was their only free day, so Sunday was the only day they could learn. He found women in the neighborhood who could teach, paid them, and opened classes in their homes. The children learned to read and to spell, and the book they read from was the Bible. They learned the catechism and went to church. They also, the accounts say, had to come with clean hands and combed hair. Raikes owned a newspaper, so he wrote about it, and the idea spread from town to town and across the sea. Tradition gives him the credit, though others had started Sunday classes before him. Behind it was a conviction that sounds obvious now and wasn't then: a poor child working in a factory was worth teaching. In Mark's Gospel, when the disciples try to shoo children away, Jesus is displeased and says: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God." In King James English, suffer means let. Let them come. Not everyone liked it. Some people worried that teaching poor children to read would make them restless. Raikes kept the schools going anyway. To him, reading was a gift, not a danger.

Bring to mind a child you know, your own, a niece, a neighbor, a student, or the child you used to be, and one small thing you know that they don't yet: how to tie a knot, how to fold a paper boat, a line of a song or a psalm. Think how you'd show it, slowly, one step at a time. If you pray, pray for that child by name; if you don't, just wish them well.
Sunday schools. Classes started on the one free day of the week, so working children could learn to read, with the Bible as their book.
Your line: every child can learn. Even on the one free day of the week. Day nine hundred fourteen.

notes: Claims rule: no dates or counts given. The index hook mentions factories; Raikes's Gloucester children worked in factories (pin-making etc.) and other trades. Confirm.
Paid women teachers in their homes, reading from the Bible, catechism and church, clean hands and combed hair: standard details in Raikes histories; confirm.
'Others had started Sunday classes before him' (e.g. Hannah Ball, Thomas Stock as co-founder); confirm.
'Suffer' as old English for 'let' is the ordinary sense of the KJV word; confirm.
'Some people worried that teaching poor children to read would make them restless': general contemporary objection; confirm.
The closing line on Protestant and Catholic reformers building schools ties back to Knox (865), Calvin (863) and Trent (872); confirm.
howItsDone: general description of Sunday school today.
